FinanceTab.title: ‘People are pissed’: union decries TSA’s removal of chairs for checkpoint staff
FinanceTab.text:
Union officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after the Trump administration unilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints.

“People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth.

TSA officials ordered that chairs be removed from travel document check stations on September 25, arguing “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism, attentiveness and active engagement with passengers” and that the policy change “reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality”.

Jones said his members had been flooded with calls and messages about the agency removing chairs.

“People are calling, members are mad, employees are upset because they literally started their day, everything was normal, and by halfway through their shift, they’re (TSA) taking all the chairs out and replacing them with inadequate mats,” said Jones. “The amount of phone calls I received is almost the same as if everybody got fired all at once, almost similar to when we have government shutdowns.”

“Our officers screen millions of people a day and they do it right, sitting or standing,” said Hydrick Thomas, president of AFGE TSA council 100, in a statement. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this.”

Jones noted the TSA checkpoint podiums are one of two places where TSA officers can rest their legs while screening passengers. Chairs were not removed from x-ray machines because the manufacturers recommend sitting while operating the machines.

Jones cited the union was not informed on the policy change and it was not negotiated, rather unilaterally implemented by the agency, and its unclear where it leaves TSA employees who require light duty accommodations.

Following the policy change, TSA workers were also required to sign a pledge that promises to support “the well-being and morale of our colleagues,” according to the union.

“They didn’t notify the union at all, obviously, nor the employees. They decided it would be a great idea to make their employees upset,” said Jones.

He said he is unsure what is being done with the chairs in airports around the US.

Jones explained the policy worsens the working conditions of TSA officers who no longer have the option of taking time off of their feet, and noted that border patrol officers and customs officers are still using chairs while screening travel documents.

US Customs and Border Patrol said it has not adopted this policy.

“A lot of people don’t have adequate footwear to need to stand up for that long,” Jones said. “The agency didn’t allow us to bargain any of these changes. They just implemented them. It’s very demoralizing, upsetting that the agency would do this to transportation security officers.”

AFGE, the largest union representing federal workers and representing TSA employees, launched a letter-writing campaign calling on the public to tell TSA to “restore the chairs”.

Union leaders criticized the policy change, TSA’s justification for it, and the agency requiring workers sign a morality pledge the same week the policy was unilaterally implemented.

“Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this,” said Thomas in a statement. “If TSA leadership truly believes standing makes people better at their jobs, I look forward to watching every manager in the building prove it for eight hours straight. We will bring the pledge. They can bring their own chair, if they are allowed one.”

The policy change is just the latest issue to impact workers at TSA under the Trump administration, who are also currently facing possible pay freezes and significant increases to their health insurance premium costs.

Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has attempted twice to cancel the collective bargaining agreement between the agency and TSA unions, with a judge ruling in January to reinstate the contract, ruling the agency’s attempt to cancel it violated a court injunction.

TSA workers also continued working during two government shutdowns without pay since Trump began his second presidential term, which included a government shutdown from 1 October to 12 November 2025, followed by a partial government shutdown that impacted TSA workers for 76 days from February to April this year.

The Trump administration has also been expanding privatization of work done by TSA workers to private contractors through the TSA Gold+ program; however, following criticism of the plan, Tampa airport abandoned its plan to join the program.

TSA did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the policy change and union’s criticisms of the policy and morale pledge. TSA still requires a chair must be available upon request for travelers.

“This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News on the policy change, but did not cite why the agency did not negotiate the change with the union.

“All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers.”

SportsTab.title: Manchester City: A statement win but does it carry weight in a season of limbo?
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City made what they will regard as a powerful statement in the most hostile territory against Liverpool at Anfield - but is it a statement that carries any weight during a Premier League season in limbo?

City's attention turned to on-field matters in their first game since being found guilty of 114 charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

The fates, and fixture list, decreed it would be at Liverpool, whose fans nurse the most burning sense of injustice after finishing second to City in 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22.

Their argument centres on the belief those titles could have been theirs had City not possessed the high finance of their Abu Dhabi-based owners, using it in the manner that led to them being investigated.

With this as the backdrop, City strode into this fevered Anfield atmosphere, with Liverpool fans high on adrenaline and determined to make their contempt for their rivals obvious - then outclassed Andoni Iraola's side in a 3-0 win.

On another day, in other circumstances, the manner of City's victory would have fed the narrative that this was a performance of champions, a winning marker laid down to their rivals as they hold a three-point lead at the top of the table.

Not here. Not in the Premier League's dysfunctional state.

Instead, once the predictable sound and fury had been diluted by City's composure and the swift realisation they were not unnerved by Anfield or the storm raging around the club, this was a surreal experience.

After the feast of excitement delivered when Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp presided over the greatest domestic rivalry of recent years, this was an occasion - remarkable as it seems - that seemed robbed of a sense of jeopardy by the circumstances surrounding it.

Yes, it was a statement display and City celebrated wildly at the final whistle, but will it count for anything given they await potential sanctions suggested including Premier League relegation or a record points deduction?

As Erling Haaland looked close to tears in front of Manchester City's fans, including his father Alf-Inge, and head coach Enzo Maresca pumped his fists in jubilation, Anfield's DJ slipped Fleetwood Mac's 'Little Lies' on to the loudspeakers in a final message of defiance.

Maresca said: "We knew there was going to be noise but we need to make our own noise by winning games. We need to learn to deal with the noise but the message is to win games.

"For me it's quite easy. I try to focus on things I can control. There are things that are not in my hands so I don't stress about them.

"I cannot control things outside football, so why stress? I stress about gameplan, day-by-day training sessions, but the rest it's not in my hands."

Haaland added: "For every single person part of Manchester City, every fan, this is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time. It was tough. It was hard, but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone.

"It's always tough to come here. If you look at the record it's tough. With the Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp era it was tough for both teams, always has been. It was important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about. The thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That's the only thing we can do."

City have appealed against the verdict, but until the dust settles and final decisions are made, this Premier League season is in a holding pattern.

When City come to Anfield and win, especially as convincingly as they did here, it should be a win without qualification or questions.

This does not apply amid the current uncertainty.

Every victory, every league table, will come with a metaphorical asterisk until clarity and finality comes. No-one knows when this will be.

City's players did their jobs to perfection, victory secured by second-half goals from Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki. It is all they can do.

There can be no escape, however, from the cloud hanging over Manchester City because every win will carry the same rider - producing a state of inertia that is not good for the Premier League.

In the end, a day that promised huge discomfort for City ended in a stroll.

City navigated the hostile reception awaiting them at Anfield by arriving through the staff and contractors' entrance - while an inevitable febrile environment awaited them.

Even the derided half-and-half scarves were doing a roaring trade, until it was noticed the sky blue half read: 'Shamchester City - The Cheats'.

The announcement of City's line-up was drowned out by deafening jeers, while banners around Anfield carried a variety of messages.

They including 'A Generation Of Supporters Cheated', 'And After All You Really Robbed Us All' and - in a nod to the Oasis song Stop Crying Your Heart Out, written by Noel Gallagher who was at Anfield, 'All Of Your Stars Are Fading Away'.

This was all watched by an impassive City chief executive Ferran Soriano, but any notion their fans would turn on the owners was dispelled by a flag reading: 'In Khaldoon We Trust. We've Won It All', a gesture of support for the embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.

City's fans also waved hundreds of inflatable bananas, an old habit when they spent time in the lower leagues in reduced circumstances. There remains the possibility they will get the chance to wave them down the tiers once more in the near future.

The first half did much to pour cold water on what started as a red-hot atmosphere, further diluted by City's second-half domination, although Liverpool's fans rammed home their disgust until the final whistle, chanting "cheat" every time their opponents passed in a lengthy period of possession.

Former Liverpool and England defender Stephen Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live: "This needs rectifying as quickly as possible, but this isn't an easy thing to come to a conclusion. It's never-ending. It's so difficult and it's going to take so long to sort out."

He added: "The hard part is that this is a brilliant Manchester City team, but you have to caveat it and say they have done it illegally and they bought their way. You're caught in what you're thinking about this City team.

"I admire them because they're so good individually and so great, but the way it has been done and put together has not been put together correctly."

While ex-Man Utd striker Wayne Rooney, added: "I know what it is like from managing Derby County when they had a points deduction. The mindset and message to the players was simple – just try to win the next game.

"All the noise around the club, from the media and other fans, will make them even hungrier to succeed.

"They could be fighting for the title or fighting for relegation by the end of the season. Who knows what's going to happen."

As City walked off, they were accompanied by the taunt of "You're going down" from the Kop.

City's fans answered with the trademark: "We're not really here."

This, in essence, is what makes this Premier League campaign one that might yet be rendered void. City might win the title - but who knows if they will be here next season?

As Maresca's side move into top gear and threaten to accelerate away from the chasing pack with wins such as this, no-one has a clue what their final destination will be.

SportsTab.title: Winless and an 'easy touch' - what's happened to the Anfield fear factor?
SportsTab.text:
It is early days but Andoni Iraola will know that if his time at Liverpool is going to be a success, then he must make Anfield a fortress again.

Right now, the struggle is real.

Liverpool were impressive for the most part against a Manchester City side that arrived on Merseyside with a 100% record.

However, once Ryan Gravenberch was sent off in the 62nd minute, they capitulated to a 3-0 defeat.

As Iraola said post-match to Match of the Day: "We played two different games. One until the red card, and then after.

"For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us."

His unbeaten start is now over. This was actually his first Premier League defeat in 24 games (W10, D13) since January, including his time at Bournemouth.

The Reds, though, are now winless in three Premier League home matches this season - although they have won at Anfield in the Champions League and Carabao Cup - for just the second time ever.

That winless run in the league at Anfield stretches back to last season with Liverpool now winless in five successive Premier League home games (D4 L1).

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The best teams in the world are also horrible to play against. Liverpool aren't horrible.

"They're an easy touch at the moment. They have too many players that are nice and they have to change that part of things.

"Liverpool have got a lot of work to do.

"They don't have enough leaders at the moment, apart from Virgil van Dijk barking orders."

Going back to the start of the year, Liverpool have won just four games in 13 Anfield Premier League matches.

In fact, they have won more matches away from home than at home during this period.

A closer look at the stats clearly shows Liverpool's home form has dropped off season by season since 2023-2024, although it is important to note this season is still a very small sample size.

Away sides have a lower win percentage at Anfield (12.5 per cent) than at any other stadium in Premier League history.

However, is this reputation starting to dwindle?

Ex-Man Utd midfielder Paul Scholes told The Good, the Bad and the Football podcast in September: "When you go to Liverpool, especially when Jurgen Klopp was there, the crowd played such a major part. It feels like that's gone… I don't think the fans are quite on board at the minute with what's happening there.

"When we used to go there, I'd think, 'how are we going to get the ball?', because they were on top of you. Teams seem to have a lot more possession and look a bit more comfortable than they ever have."

And Scholes' former team-mate Nicky Butt added: "The likes of Fulham five years ago are going to Anfield and they're beaten before they even go up the steps."

While Liverpool have won twice on their travels this season, they now sit ninth in the league - and their main issue seems fairly clear.

They have scored just seven goals this season - just twice at Anfield - and only seven teams have managed fewer.

It was early on in the first half when the cameras panned to Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai in the Main Stand at Anfield - all three of them were out with injuries.

Among them, the trio have scored six of Liverpool's seven league goals this season and on a day when Man City's attack showed their class, Liverpool didn't show any quality in the final third.

City (16) have scored more than double the goals Liverpool (7) have scored this season in the top flight.

Across three league games at Anfield this season, Liverpool have failed to score in two of them. That must improve.

In Isak's absence, Lewis Koumas put in a great shift. However, the 21-year-old lacks that killer edge in front of goal at this level.

The focus must fall on Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. It is this kind of game where you need a match-winning moment and neither showed anywhere near the quality that is expected when you have a price tag of over £100m.

There was one moment at 0-0 in the 55th minute when Wirtz had Milos Kerkez and Barcola in acres of space to his left, but chose to shoot and fired wide.

"You learn a lot in games like today," Iraola said. "I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It's a loss and we didn't get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot."

But deep down, Iraola will know there is a lot of work to do and getting the big money signings to deliver will be high on his agenda.

SportsTab.title: Singapore Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Kimi Antonelli moves to brink of title
SportsTab.text:
Lewis Hamilton apologised to his Ferrari team after overriding the pit wall and choosing his own strategy during the Singapore Grand Prix.

Ferrari were on course to finish second and third with Charles Leclerc and Hamilton, but instead the seven-time champion fell back to sixth in the closing laps as he fought a losing battle to hold off three cars while on fading tyres.

Hamilton apologised to the team over the radio on the slowing-down lap after the race, saying: "Sorry, boys. I let you down today with that strategy. My call, and I lost us valuable points. I'll try and make up for it in the next one."

Team principal Frederic Vasseur said: "Clearly we asked them to pit. Charles pitted. Lewis didn't want to pit because he... I don't know why. And then he realised it was the wrong call. It's why he apologised to the team.

"Now it's not a drama for me that he made the wrong call. I'm making mistakes, he's making mistakes, we're all making mistakes sometimes. Now we have to look ahead and make mistakes positively."

Hamilton did not speak to the media after the race after saying he felt unwell and being given permission to miss the interview zone, known as the media pen.

In a statement released by Ferrari, he said: "Under the virtual safety car, the team called me in but I missed the entry. After that, I decided to stay out and try to hold track position to the end but in the closing laps, I was struggling massively with tyre degradation and lost three places, finishing P6, which doesn't reflect the pace we had in the car.

"A painful lesson, but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made. Not every call will work out, and I can accept getting it wrong but I'm sorry for the team for the points we lost today. They put so much into every weekend, and I wanted to deliver more for them. I'll continue to put the work in and come back fighting at the next race."

Ferrari called both cars in to the pits during a virtual safety car that was called mid-race. Stopping under the VSC saves about 10 seconds versus stopping under racing conditions.

Hamilton said in the statement that his decision was based on his improved pace on the soft-compound tyre after he had been forced to make an earlier pit stop than planned because the medium tyre on which he started the race was not performing.

"At a track [where it's] difficult to overtake, you need to try something different and I chose to start on a new medium tyre, to go long and try to make a one-stop work," he said.

"Unfortunately the medium didn't perform as well as the soft. I had a good second stint and the pace was back, but I couldn't make the progress I needed."

His first stop was six laps before Leclerc's and when the Monegasque emerged on to the track, Hamilton was right behind him and initially faster.

At one stage, he pointed out to the team that he had "lost two seconds on that lap", but the team decided not to invert the cars. Hamilton followed Leclerc within two seconds for a further 10 laps before slowly starting to lose ground a couple of laps before the VSC.

Vasseur said the team decided to leave Leclerc in front because he had pitted later than Hamilton.

"The tyre advantage was for Charles, that he pitted six laps later," Vasseur said. "I think it was the right call."

However, that argument appears to be somewhat undermined by the fact that the medium tyre emerged as the worst option for the race - as Hamilton had found out in the first stint and other drivers later discovered.

Leclerc was put back on the soft when he stopped under the VSC.

Hamilton's error means Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli is in a position to clinch his first world title at the next race, the US Grand Prix in Austin, after finishing third behind race winner Max Verstappen and Leclerc.

Antonelli's lead over team-mate George Russell, who finished ninth after starting from the back of the grid, has extended to 102 points and 111 over Hamilton.

The Italian needs to leave Austin with an advantage of at least 125 points to clinch the title, with five races at most remaining after that.

He will do so if he wins the race with Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower at the Circuit of the Americas on 25 October.

If he becomes champion this year, the 20-year-old will be the youngest in Formula 1 history.

Asked if he would be daring to dream about the title on the flight home, he said: "For sure, but at the same time, I know it's very close, I know it's there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can.

"The mindset is always the same, to go out there and win and perform the best way I can.

"This weekend I haven't particularly driven that well. I felt like I could have done a better job, but I feel confident that a week to reset and I'm really looking forward to being back in Austin.

"But at the end of the day, if I don't do my job well, then the result won't come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that."

There is some doubt about the mathematics of the championship because it is not completely clear how many races are remaining.

F1 is pushing ahead with the original schedule, which ends with two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, despite the war in the Middle East, having been reassured the countries are safe.

But if the war intensifies before mid-November, those races will have to be cancelled. In that event, the season would end at Imola in Italy, on the same 6 December date as Abu Dhabi, after a two-week break following the Las Vegas race on 22 November.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "I haven't looked at it from that perspective, because the moment I have the thought of 'how many points is it actually, and when could he win it,' I remind myself that this is motor racing and crazy things have happened.

"The aim must be to score points, not to lose too many on the others, like today, gaining on Lewis, which was unexpected, and then it's going to come towards him, whether that's in Mexico or Brazil [immediately after Austin] or further down the line."

Mercedes split their cars between two different specifications in Singapore in an attempt to understand why a major upgrade introduced at the previous race in Malaysia did not work.

Antonelli drove the new spec and Russell the old, and by the end of the weekend the team said they had made some progress in understanding the new aerodynamic package.

Antonelli said: "We're just trying to understand how to extract more potential out of it because we do see the gains, we do see what it could bring.

"It's just that the window is very small at the moment where the car operates and is very sensitive to the way you drive it, the way you take a corner, the way you brake. So it reacts very differently.

"So hopefully now in Austin, we have three free practices, so we can be very open-minded with set-up and hopefully we can find a way and we can use the full potential of the package and finally see the gains."

Russell was asked how he viewed the rest of the season now the championship was almost over. He replied: "The goal is to improve the car. We were dominant for so long and since the break we have seen Red Bull be exceptionally fast on many different types of circuits and we need to go back to winning ways."

Verstappen's victory was his first grand prix win in Singapore. It was also his second in succession, emphasising Red Bull's return to the front after a difficult start to the season.

"Very different tracks that we have gone well at now. That's of course always nice to see," said the 29-year-old.

"Our car has taken a really nice step forward. It's just been more driveable and more predictable. That's what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front. And I hope that we can carry that momentum forward.

"We don't really have anything to win in the championship, right? Kimi is miles ahead. I don't care if I'm second, third or fourth. It doesn't do anything. But I just want to have fun until the end, you know, try to go for a day's success."

But the four-time champion was cautious about the prospect of being competitive at every race before the end of the season.

"It's very difficult to say and I don't want to say now that I will be in the fight in Austin," he said.

"Yeah, the last few weekends have been great. But I just take it race by race and once we are in Austin, then we'll see how it will go there. But it's again a very different track.

"From what I saw in WEC (the World Endurance Championship), the track is incredibly bumpy. Oh my God, yeah, I'll probably need to order a new spine, I think, after the weekend. Yeah, I'll become like Robocop. Yeah, crazy. That's again a new challenge for everyone, to deal with those bumps.

"And then we just go from there. We have to go to Mexico, high altitude, everything will run super hot, and we need to see how the engine is going to perform in that altitude, how the car is behaving, because it's very different.

"So there are so many different things that you can get right or wrong in those races."

SportsTab.title: Man City: Prime Minister Andy Burnham to release details of his meetings with Man City owners
SportsTab.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.

Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

"I've been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do and I'm going to," Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast.

"I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up following the guilty verdict before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".

However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict.

City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0.

Burnham was mayor of Manchester from 2017 until earlier this year and his tenure took place during a sustained period of success for City.

As mayor, he championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester's economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city's leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

"I don't think I misspoke," said Burnham of his past comments on Man City's owners.

"What I would say is my mind hadn't been on all of the issues. My mind had been on Labour Party conference and I was doing interviews in relation to it.

"And also, I didn't link those two things. You know, the questions linked those two things. What I would say is they're very separate.

"The football issues are different from the investment issues. People will try and conflate those two things, but they shouldn't, in my view.

"The football issues, the findings of the independent commission are serious, as I said in the interview."

The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League.

An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.

The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".

A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.

SportsTab.title: Australia v South Africa: Pace attack and Steve Smith put tourists in charge
SportsTab.text:
First Test, Durban (day three of five)

Australia 390 & 33-0: Maddinson 17*

South Africa 284: Bedingham 49; Cummins 3-54

Australia lead by 139 runs

Australia's modern Test side remain a fascinating one to unpick.

Viewed by many in England as there for the taking in last winter's Ashes despite a 4-1 win, they are also labelled too old by many observers at home.

The victims of recent shock defeats by West Indies and Bangladesh, they are still unbeaten in their past nine Test series.

But while their struggling batting line-up was bailed out by Matt Renshaw across the first two days of the first Test in Durban, they took control over South Africa on day three in an all-too familiar way.

Nine years after they first appeared together as Australia's bowling quartet, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon produced their latest relentless performance to dismiss South Africa for 284. There was even some magic from Steve Smith thrown in too.

Cummins took three wickets, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon two apiece, in doing so brushing off any doubts about their effectiveness at the start of a run of Tests against the world Test champions, in-form New Zealand, India and England.

At 82-1 in response to Australia's 390, South Africa appeared well in the Test on a relatively good surface.

Australia's bowlers searched for early swing and Aiden Markram and David Bedingham countered with a second-wicket partnership which progressed at almost 4.5 runs per over.

It was then, at the 20-over mark, captain Cummins reverted to Australia's tried and tested - Lyon one end, the quicks rotating at the other.

Having bowled 34% of their deliveries full in the first 20 overs, Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins dragged back their lengths. There were only 19 deliveries pitched fuller than six metres between the 20th and 60th overs.

With deliveries easy to hit scarce, Markram and Bedingham attempted forced back-foot drives and edged to slip for 37 and 49 respectively.

Wiaan Mulder was caught in two minds and bounced out by Cummins. Tristan Stubbs top-edged the Australia captain to fine leg.

In Australia's first innings, Renshaw, who ground out a superb 190, faced 52 deliveries pitched as short and played a pull or hook shot to four of them. He scored runs with only one of those shots - when he had 176 runs to his name and had faced 368 balls.

The contrast to Renshaw's application could not have been greater.

Six overs after Stubbs was caught, Marco Jansen, who had struck six fours in quickly reaching 26, also tried to pull Hazlewood off a fuller length and was tamely caught at mid-off.

The quality of the bowling and fact the Proteas are playing their first Test since November were other factors in South Africa's slide.

At the other end, off-spinner Lyon bowled 19 overs at less than three runs per over.

The 39-year-old had a more worn pitch to utilise than South Africa's spinners and found significantly more turn and threat.

He also had the sprawling Steve Smith to his advantage.

Both of Smith's catches off Lyon, first to dismiss Temba Bavuma and then Kyle Verreynne, were feats of anticipation. He saw both right-handers shape to reverse sweep, gambled and clung on at close range. The first was good. The one-handed second was spectacular.

"He's an absolute freak," said Lyon. "He practices that in training.

"He is an incredible thinker of the game but the way he moves, premeditates, for those types of catches.

"There are not many people in the dressing room that would be able to pull off those two catches."

In between, Smith's leaping catch at second slip after Cummins found Bedingham's edge took the 37-year-old back above Joe Root as the non-wicketkeeper with the most catches in Test history on 223.

While he ended the day with three more catches than Root, he still has a catch percentage about 77%, which sits below the format average.

He creates, and occasionally drops, chances such as these - chances others would not have created.

The result is Australia's fabled foursome now have 607 wickets in Tests in which they have played as a quartet.

The next most successful bowling four-pronged attack is James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Ben Stokes and Moeen Ali, who took 415 wickets in their 31 Tests together for England.

"Each of these players will go down as a legend of Australian cricket," said former Australia bowler Jason Gillespie on ABC Radio.

"Starc got hit for a few early but I didn't mind that.

"Hazlewood was very good, as he always is. Cummins was hostile. He looked fresh."

Much has been made of Australia's ageing side and a perceived lack of succession planning.

At 37, Starc is the oldest of the three quicks but his average pace of 141.21km/h in 2026 is higher than any of his past three years. He is also averaging his most swing in a calendar year since 2015.

The concern for Australia comes when they are not fit, with Hazlewood having missed all five of last winter's Ashes Tests and Cummins four.

Australia's issue right now is keeping each of their quartet on the field, because they appear as good as ever.

At 33-0, Australia lead South Africa by 139 runs.

Even with bad light halting play early again, they should have the time to press home an advantage across the Test's final two days.

SportsTab.title: Singapore Grand Prix: Harry Benjamin's driver ratings as Max Verstappen wins again
SportsTab.text:
Max Verstappen took his second win in a row with victory from pole position at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The Dutchman also won the final sprint event of the campaign at Marina Bay and has moved up two places in the drivers' standings from sixth to fourth.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished third and has extended his title advantage over Mercedes team-mate George Russell, who was ninth, to 102 points.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Singapore.

Max Verstappen - 10/10

Pretty much the definition of a perfect weekend. Pole and victory in both the sprint race and grand prix, and once George Russell crashed out of the sprint on Saturday there was barely a moment where Red Bull's Verstappen looked like losing control of either race.

Charles Leclerc- 9/10

Consistently Verstappen's closest challenger and took two podiums from the weekend. Third in the sprint followed by second in the grand prix was about as much as Ferrari could realistically have asked for.

Kimi Antonelli - 8.5/10

Another hugely mature weekend from Mercedes' championship leader. Fourth in the sprint and fourth in qualifying before fighting his way on to the grand prix podium late on, despite dealing with brake concerns and flirting a little too often with track limits.

Lando Norris - 6.5/10

Sunday was solid enough, with fourth probably the maximum McLaren had on outright pace. But his collision with team-mate Oscar Piastri in the sprint cost both drivers heavily, and prevents this from being rated as a particularly strong weekend.

Oscar Piastri - 7/10

The victim rather than the instigator of McLaren's sprint collision and recovered with a decent Sunday performance. A slow puncture forced an extra stop but he still chased down and passed Lewis Hamilton for fifth, although seventh in qualifying left him with plenty of work to do.

Lewis Hamilton - 7.5/10

His Saturday was excellent - a brilliant start helped turn sixth into second in the sprint before he qualified third for the main race. Ran in the podium places for much of Sunday too, but his decision to stay out on worn tyres backfired badly and eventually dropped him to sixth.

Liam Lawson - 8.5/10

A really impressive weekend for Racing Bulls' Lawson. Fifth in the sprint, ninth on the grand prix grid and seventh on Sunday meant points in both races and another reminder of just how strong his recent form has become.

Nico Hulkenberg - 8/10

Another very useful weekend for Audi. Took points with seventh in the sprint, narrowly missed Q3 and then finished eighth in the grand prix, holding Russell behind late on in the process.

George Russell - 7/10

The pace deserved a much higher score. Fastest in practice, second in sprint qualifying and sensational off the line to take the sprint lead. However, throwing it into the wall at the end of lap one was a major mistake. Recovering from 19th on the grand prix grid to ninth was an excellent response from the Mercedes driver.

Isack Hadjar - 8/10

Almost everything that went wrong before Sunday was outside of his control. Mechanical trouble on his Red Bull ended his sprint and reliability problems meant he couldn't set a qualifying time, so recovering from the pit lane to score a point was an excellent drive.

Pierre Gasly - 7/10

Eighth in qualifying was one of the stronger midfield performances of Saturday. Just missed the points in both races and comfortably led Alpine's challenge across the weekend, even if there wasn't quite enough race pace to convert it.

Oliver Bearman - 7.5/10

A particularly good sprint where he produced a smart move on Gasly and came home sixth. He qualified P12 and the grand prix was less spectacular, but scoring three sprint points still made this a useful weekend for Haas' Bearman.

Esteban Ocon - 6/10

Finished 10th in the sprint and 13th in the grand prix without ever really looking like threatening Haas team-mate Bearman's points haul. A fairly anonymous weekend in which Briton Bearman had the upper hand.

Carlos Sainz - 5.5/10

Starting the sprint from the pit lane immediately made life difficult and there was little improvement afterwards. Qualified in 14th and finished there, making this another frustrating weekend for Williams.

Arvid Lindblad - 5.5/10

There was obvious pace in qualifying, where he reached Q3, but the rest of the weekend was a lot messier for the Racing Bulls driver. Spinning to the back in the sprint and then slipping from 10th to 15th on Sunday meant the potential never really translated into a result.

Fernando Alonso - 5/10

Aston Martin had hoped Singapore would suit the car but it never materialised. Alonso was only 17th in qualifying and finished there on Sunday after an equally quiet sprint.

Sergio Perez - 4.5/10

Another difficult weekend for Cadillac. His sprint ended almost immediately after contact with Lance Stroll, and 20th in qualifying left him with little chance of recovering on Sunday, eventually finishing 17th.

A messy sprint included the three-car incident with Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas before the Williams driver eventually retired. Qualifying 17th didn't offer much encouragement either, and another retirement late in the grand prix completed a poor weekend.

Valtteri Bottas - 4/10

Caught up in the sprint collision involving Albon and Bortoleto, before qualifying 21st for the grand prix in his Cadillac. Reaching the finish on Sunday was about the only positive, three laps behind the winner.

Lance Stroll - 4.5/10

His sprint was over on the opening lap after the collision with Perez, for which neither driver was penalised. Qualified 19th before a clutch problem ended his race midway through.

Franco Colapinto - 5/10

Not much chance to build any momentum across the weekend. Retired early from the sprint, hit the wall on his final qualifying lap and then suffered a suspected driveline or gearbox-related technical issue on his Alpine in the grand prix.

Gabriel Bortoleto - 5/10

His sprint retirement came in the three-car accident with Albon and Bottas, so there wasn't much he could do about that. P15 in qualifying was less impressive, before another early retirement on Sunday brought a frustrating weekend to an end for the Audi man.

SportsTab.title: NFL roundup: Daniels’ overtime blunder costs Commanders as Giants salvage wild 27-27 tie
SportsTab.text:
Jayden Daniels took off on an ill-advised scramble in the closing seconds of overtime with the Commanders in field-goal range, and Washington were unable to stop the clock before time expired, settling for a 27-27 tie with the New York Giants on Sunday after both teams made critical mistakes in the extra period.

Washington (1-3-1) got the ball with two minutes left in overtime when Daron Payne stripped the ball from Cam Skattebo with the Giants in range for a game-winning field goal. Daniels quickly moved the Commanders to the Giants’ 24-yard line, but with 12 seconds left and Washington out of timeouts, he held on to the ball and went down for no gain. Washington lined up to spike the ball, but the clock ticked down to zero and coach Dan Quinn ripped off his headset in disgust.

The Commanders had led by two touchdowns in the fourth quarter before Jameis Winston led a furious comeback for the NFC East-leading Giants (3-1-1). He connected with Isaiah Likely for a 17-yard touchdown midway through the fourth quarter – Likely’s second touchdown catch of the game – and then found Malik Nabers for the tying score, also from 17 yards, with 1:43 remaining.

Winston finished with 326 passing yards and three touchdowns. Daniels threw for 199 yards and rushed for 103 yards and two touchdowns while wearing a brace on his left elbow in his first game back since dislocating it for the second time in Week 2.

On a dreary, rainy day at Northwest Stadium, the Giants struggled offensively in the first half but found their rhythm late as Winston led New York to scores on four consecutive possessions.

But the Giants also made too many mistakes to come away with the victory. New York’s kicking problems proved costly, with Dominic Zvada converting only two of his five field-goal attempts.

Meanwhile, the Giants’ defense struggled to contain Daniels, who rushed for two second-half touchdowns – a 38-yard run in the third quarter that made it 19-6 and a 26-yard score in the fourth that gave the Commanders a seemingly comfortable 27-13 lead.

But the Giants rallied behind Winston and his two leading targets, Nabers (11 catches for 121 yards and a touchdown) and Likely (11 receptions for 94 yards and two touchdowns). On his second score, Likely had the ball punched out just after crossing the goal line, but the touchdown was upheld after a replay review.

After Nabers’ tying touchdown, the Commanders had one last chance to win in regulation, but their drive stalled at midfield.

Las Vegas Raiders 17-45 New England Patriots

Drake Maye threw four touchdown passes and ran for another score as the New England Patriots rolled past the Las Vegas Raiders 45-17 on Sunday.

Maye completed 26 of 34 passes for 374 yards in the second 300-yard game of his career. Two touchdowns went to Pop Douglas and one each to Hunter Henry and Kyle Williams. Rhamondre Stevenson added a touchdown run.

Maye became the first New England quarterback to throw at least three touchdown passes in consecutive games since Tom Brady in 2018. It was also his first turnover-free game of the season. He scored on a three-yard run.

The Patriots (3-2) finished with a season-high 536 yards and forced a fumble despite playing without injured receiver Mack Hollins and cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III.

Kirk Cousins completed 19 of 28 passes for 243 yards, including a touchdown to Brock Bowers that briefly pulled the Raiders (3-2) level. But Las Vegas did not reach the end zone again until the fourth quarter after scoring at least 26 points in each of their first four games.

New York Jets 17-12 Cleveland Browns

Braelon Allen ran 22 yards for the go-ahead touchdown late in the fourth quarter after New York recovered a fumbled punt snap, and the Jets ended a three-game skid with a 17-12 victory over the Cleveland Browns on a rain-soaked Sunday.

Rookie David Bailey had three of New York’s eight sacks of Deshaun Watson, and Geno Smith threw a touchdown pass to Garrett Wilson on the Jets’ opening drive, helping snap the Browns’ three-game winning streak.

The Browns had a final chance when they got the ball with 1:41 left and no timeouts. But New York’s defense, as they had all game, stiffened and sealed the victory when Will McDonald strip-sacked Watson on fourth down and recovered the fumble.

Smith completed 17 of 30 passes for 182 yards and the touchdown to Wilson, who had seven catches for 104 yards. Allen ran for 116 yards and the winning touchdown on 24 carries.

It wasn’t pretty, with steady rain falling throughout the game as the remnants of Hurricane Isaias blew through the north-east. But the struggling Jets (2-3) were able to bounce back after surrendering a fourth-quarter lead.

Pittsburgh Steelers 34-22 Indianapolis Colts

Jaylen Warren piled up 188 total yards and two long touchdowns – one rushing and one receiving – to lead the Pittsburgh Steelers past the Indianapolis Colts 34-22 on Sunday.

The Steelers (3-2) shook off a loss at Cleveland by relying on Warren and a defense that frequently bent but rarely broke.

Warren caught six passes for 87 yards, including an 80-yard catch-and-run touchdown in the first quarter, and added 101 yards on the ground, highlighted by a 50-yard sprint to the end zone in the third quarter. The typically low-key former undrafted free agent celebrated by hurdling across the goal line.

Aaron Rodgers completed 22 of 31 passes for 235 yards and three touchdowns. While Warren did most of the work on their 80-yard connection, the 42-year-old Rodgers absorbed a crushing hit from 314lb Colts defensive tackle Grover Stewart as he released the ball.

Pat Freiermuth caught five passes for 44 yards and two touchdowns for Pittsburgh, the second a 17-yard pass from Rodgers with 6:40 remaining that gave the Steelers enough breathing room to beat the Colts for the 10th time in 12 meetings.

Houston Texans 26-3 Tennessee Titans

CJ Stroud threw for 261 yards and a touchdown and ran for another score as the Houston Texans snapped their winless start to the season by routing the Tennessee Titans 26-3 on Sunday.

It was the second straight season Houston (1-4) ended an opening winless skid by beating Tennessee. This time, the Texans forced two turnovers and Will Anderson Jr had three of Houston’s four sacks. Ka’imi Fairbairn kicked four field goals as the Texans took a 12-3 halftime lead.

Houston dominated the second and third quarters, outgaining the Titans 225-49 and outscoring them 16-0. The Texans held Tennessee to a season-low 187 total yards.

The Titans (0-5) have now lost 11 straight games in the AFC South and six straight overall dating back to the end of last season.

Tennessee led only after opening the game with a drive that ended in a 30-yard field goal by Joey Slye. Cam Ward finished with 170 passing yards.

The Texans then forced a three-and-out before safety Jalen Pitre recovered a Tyjae Spears fumble on Tennessee’s next possession. Jake Hansen intercepted Ward on the ensuing drive, and Houston followed by forcing another three-and-out.

Minnesota Vikings 23-13 New Orleans Saints

Justin Jefferson marked his return to Minnesota’s lineup with a leaping touchdown catch, Aaron Jones made up for an early fumble with a pivotal fourth-quarter score and the Vikings remained unbeaten with a 23-13 victory over the slumping New Orleans Saints on Sunday.

Will Reichard made all three of his field-goal attempts from 40 yards or more for the Vikings (5-0), including a 55-yarder that put Minnesota ahead by 10 in the fourth quarter and all but condemned the Saints (1-4) to a third straight loss, all at the Superdome.

Jones finished with 113 rushing yards on 25 carries. Jefferson, who sat out Week 4 with an ankle injury, caught six passes for 79 yards from Kyler Murray, who threw for 229 yards and a touchdown without a turnover and rushed for 51 yards.

The Vikings, who entered the game allowing an NFL-low 12.8 points per game, surrendered only one offensive touchdown and held New Orleans to 142 yards.

Safety Jonas Sanker returned a fumble 87 yards for the Saints’ other touchdown.

Cincinnati Bengals 31-24 Miami Dolphins

Joe Burrow threw four touchdown passes, safety Jordan Battle had two interceptions and the Cincinnati Bengals beat the Miami Dolphins 31-24 on Sunday.

Ja’Marr Chase, who had been questionable after suffering a concussion last week against Jacksonville, caught six passes for 77 yards, including a spectacular one-handed, 45-yard touchdown catch that made it 28-10.

Burrow completed 23 of 32 passes for 190 yards and also threw touchdowns to tight ends Mike Gesicki and Tanner Hudson and running back Samaje Perine. The Bengals quarterback exploited the Dolphins’ young secondary, completing passes to nine different receivers.

Battle intercepted Malik Willis on consecutive drives in the second quarter. The safety had said earlier in the week that he had spotted a tell in Willis’s throwing motion, pointing out that the Dolphins quarterback appeared to tap the ball before releasing it.

The Dolphins (0-5) pulled within seven points with 45 seconds remaining on Willis’s one-yard touchdown run, set up by a 23-yard catch by rookie Kevin Coleman Jr, who had also caught a touchdown earlier in the fourth quarter. Riley Patterson struck the left upright with the extra-point attempt, and the ensuing onside kick went out of bounds as Cincinnati snapped their two-game skid.

Green Bay Packers 31-7 Chicago Bears

Christian Watson caught two long touchdown passes from Jordan Love, MarShawn Lloyd also scored twice and the Green Bay Packers exacted a measure of revenge against the Chicago Bears with a 31-7 rout on Sunday.

Love completed 25 of 31 passes for 367 yards, the most by a Packers quarterback against the Bears at Lambeau Field. He connected with Watson on a 42-yard touchdown in the first quarter and a 53-yarder in the third.

Green Bay had lost three of their previous four meetings with Chicago and squandered a 21-3 halftime lead in a 31-27 NFC wild-card playoff defeat last season. Caleb Williams celebrated that comeback victory by grating cheese on the field, mocking Green Bay’s Cheesehead fanbase.

Williams missed a third straight game on Sunday with a hamstring injury, leaving Tyson Bagent to start in his place. Xavier McKinney intercepted two of Bagent’s passes as the Packers forced five turnovers.

Detroit Lions 45-21 Arizona Cardinals

Jared Goff threw three touchdown passes, Jahmyr Gibbs added 151 yards rushing and two more scores, and the Detroit Lions shook off a slow start by scoring 31 unanswered points to roll past the Arizona Cardinals 45-21 on Sunday.

Gibbs barreled into the end zone on a one-yard run in the second quarter and added a three-yard touchdown run in the fourth, bouncing off the offensive line before reversing field and finding room to run. The three-time Pro Bowl selection has scored an NFL-record 58 touchdowns before his 25th birthday, surpassing Lions great Barry Sanders, who had 57.

Jameson Williams had his first game with multiple touchdown receptions, catching scoring passes of eight and 39 yards for Detroit (3-2).

Arizona (1-4) have lost nine straight home games, a streak stretching back more than a year.

It was a disappointing, bizarre afternoon for the Cardinals, who finalized a trade to send receiver Marvin Harrison Jr to the Houston Texans midway through the first quarter. Harrison was one of the team’s five inactive players against the Lions and was not seen at the stadium.

Denver Broncos 23-17 Los Angeles Chargers

Wil Lutz kicked a go-ahead 19-yard field goal with 5:07 remaining, lifting the Denver Broncos to a 23-17 victory over the winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday.

Lutz’s 36-yarder with 1:08 left extended the lead and capped a run of 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter for the Broncos (3-2).

Denver earned their first division win and first victory at SoFi Stadium since 2023, with coach Sean Payton calling the plays. He took those duties away from offensive coordinator Davis Webb earlier in the week. The Broncos won without injured cornerbacks Pat Surtain II (ankle) and Riley Moss (ribs).

The Chargers also started 0-5 in 2023, the year before coach Jim Harbaugh took over. They came in with a decimated offensive line featuring four rookies trying to protect quarterback Justin Herbert, who completed 14 of 24 passes for 121 yards, a touchdown and an interception while being sacked five times.

Courtland Sutton caught a five-yard touchdown pass from Bo Nix, tying the score at 17 midway through the fourth quarter. The Broncos got the ball back after Herbert came up short on fourth-and-one, and the Chargers sputtered the rest of the way.

San Francisco 49ers 32-29 Seattle Seahawks

Brock Purdy engineered two scoring drives in the fourth quarter as the San Francisco 49ers rallied to beat the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 on Sunday, with Eddy Piñeiro kicking a 43-yard field goal with 1:56 remaining.

The win for the 49ers (5-0) offered a measure of revenge for their two late-season losses to Seattle (3-2) last season, including a 41-6 defeat in the divisional round of the playoffs with a short-handed roster.

San Francisco were healthier for the first meeting this season, and Purdy delivered late as the 49ers opened with five straight wins for the third time in eight seasons.

The game featured an NFL season-high seven combined turnovers, the ejection of 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw and no touchdown drives of more than 25 yards before San Francisco took over trailing 26-21 late in the third quarter.

Purdy responded with an impressive drive against Seattle’s vaunted defense, including a 28-yard pass to Mike Evans after an intentional grounding penalty left the 49ers facing second-and-21.

Baltimore Ravens 30-23 Atlanta Falcons (OT)

Tyler Huntley led Baltimore to a game-tying touchdown and two-point conversion in the final minute of regulation, then scored on a 1-yard sneak in overtime as the Ravens rallied to beat the Atlanta Falcons 30-23 on Sunday night.

Derrick Henry ran for 102 yards against the Falcons’ top-ranked run defense for the Ravens (4-1).

After Michael Penix Jr left the game with a rib injury late in the fourth quarter, Tua Tagovailoa took over at quarterback for the Falcons (2-3) in overtime. Tagovailoa’s pass intended for Drake London was intercepted by Kyle Hamilton to end the game.

Huntley completed 24 of 32 passes for 201 yards and two touchdowns as the replacement starter for Lamar Jackson, who has an ankle injury.

Penix overcame a slow start to throw for 240 yards and a touchdown but could only watch from the bench with a towel over his head as the Ravens put the game away.

TechnologyTab.title: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says
TechnologyTab.text:
Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.

Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.

His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.

But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."

Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology its a threat to humanity.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated.

"Let's get started today," he said.

He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.

He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology.

"We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."

Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute, external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute.

"In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."

Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.

Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".

However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU.

"In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said.

"When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived.

"Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."

TechnologyTab.title: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
TechnologyTab.text:
Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.

The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.

Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.

Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.

Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.

TechnologyTab.title: Burnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts
TechnologyTab.text:
Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job.

In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.

He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff.

Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last.

Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months.

Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff.

He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation."

Referencing a landmark 1995 court ruling that is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector".

Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".

It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported by Politico, external and The Financial Times, external, alongside the Budget on 28 October.

Responding to the prime minister's comments, the Recruitment and Employment Confederation warned against "sweeping" changes to non-compete rules, adding they played a "vital role" in protecting commercially sensitive information and client relationships.

The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban, external on non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally.

The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy.

He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment.

He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy.

He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fund launched in Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region.

He also hinted that the government was looking at the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies.

He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them."

"So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale."

TechnologyTab.title: King Charles warns malicious online actors are evolving their tactics
TechnologyTab.text:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

TechnologyTab.title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
TechnologyTab.text:
An artificial intelligence (AI) agent developed by Anthropic went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the 18 July tip was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation - but the force criticised the tech firm for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

It said the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.

Citing Anthropic, the police department said its AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites when it had sent the fake tip.

The company behind the Claude chatbot discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.

But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."

The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.

But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide", the force said.

Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.

Organisations that had been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.

The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.

US President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will co-ordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers and religious groups.

Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, OpenAI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.

TechnologyTab.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
TechnologyTab.text:
It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.

It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.

The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.

But that is exactly what we have come to find.

After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.

I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.

"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."

It doesn't take long.

"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.

Three months after the fire first ignited, heat is still being detected beneath the ground.

We make our way towards the coordinates identified by the drone, and at first, there is almost nothing to see.

Then we feel it.

The soil is warm. A rock Pete picks up from the ground is, too.

Nearby, after scraping away a thin layer of earth, smoke begins to rise.

"It's really now cooking away," Pete says.

"Without the thermal technology we would be totally blind to this."

The wildfire began in the middle of July and burned across about 3,300 hectares – 33 sq km – of land, according to the Cairngorms National Park Authority.

At the height of the emergency, five experienced drone pilots were brought together to provide aerial information to the agencies fighting the fire.

Pete describes it as one of the most challenging environments he has ever flown in, with "multiple walls of flame", personnel and vehicles moving around the site and helicopters operating overhead.

Now the challenge is different.

The dramatic flames have disappeared, but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.

Each one found by the drones is reported to the land manager. They send teams who can dig into the ground and douse it with water.

For Ben Jones, senior site manager for the RSPB at Abernethy, knowing exactly where to send those teams has been crucial.

"We've been fighting this fire for over two months now and obviously we've got limited resources in terms of the number of people we have and we can't send everybody out everywhere all the time," he says.

"So we really need to know where these specific hot spots are - where we should be sending people - so that they can be as efficient as possible."

And despite the arrival of colder, wetter weather, the remaining fires cannot simply be ignored.

"Each of these hot spots has got the potential to reignite a larger fire," Ben says.

"Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says.

"It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet."

And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job.

Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape.

Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes.

"This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says.

There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread.

Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical.

"It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says.

Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot.

Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot.

Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil.

Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish.

Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning.

TechnologyTab.title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
TechnologyTab.text:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.

Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.

The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.

It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.

Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".

The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.

The BBC has approached him for comment.

A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.

Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.

University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".

"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.

Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".

"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.
